chapter: Working with Duke and final reflections
title: Duke head over heels in music, and Vodery and Luther Henderson
summary: Whaley sums up Duke as head over heels in music, praises Vodery writing amid noise, and recalls Luther Henderson watching him orchestrate at the Lafayette.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, that's a beautiful way to wind this up, Tom. I just want to thank you and if there's anything else you want to say about this great man, who was your friend ...
He was head over heels into music.
Duke Ellington -- head over heels in music, and talking to Tom Whaley who is the Chairman of the Board.

That's right -- my man, to me one of the greatest. You call the man up, Bill Vodery, I used to think he was the greatest, see, but I didn't hang around Bill too much, see, because he had another guy, the sergeant -- did you remember him?

Anyway, I thought Bill Vodery was great, stand up there and write with all that going on. Well, I did it myself at the Lafayette Theatre; I sat there and I used to orchestrate and Luther Henderson, he says he saw me doing that -- this was before Luther got big, you
know, and Luther said he saw me writing among all that turmoil and he said that was great.

And then he went on and became great himself.
Luther Henderson.
Yeah, he's the orchestrator for Ain't Misbehavin', the Fats Waller Show, Luther is.
He's the orchestrator of Ain't Misbehavin', the Fats Waller show. Henderson wrote that.
Yeah. He was around there with Fats and I, and he used to kid me.
